issue.issue_text: Whether the Test Identification Parade (TIP) was correctly relied upon.

facts: A Test Identification Parade (TIP) was conducted in which a key witness, PW-17, specifically identified one of the accused (A-6).
The trial court and the High Court both relied on the TIP, with the High Court considering it to be "without blemish".
The appellants argued that the TIP was illegal, suggesting a witness had an opportunity to see the accused before the parade.
The Magistrate (PW-9) who conducted the TIP was not cross-examined at trial regarding these allegations of illegality.

The identification of the accused was also supported by other corroborating evidence, including the recovery of a Bolero vehicle, ransom money, and a rifle from the appellant's house, all of which were linked to the crime by witnesses.
law: A TIP is part of the investigation stage and is not a mandatory requirement under the Code. Failure to hold one does not make in-court identification inadmissible.
A TIP is not substantive evidence in itself but is a tool to test and strengthen the trustworthiness of a witness's sworn testimony in court.
It is considered a "safe rule of prudence" to look for corroboration of in-court identification, such as a prior TIP, especially when the accused is a stranger to the witness.
However, this rule has exceptions, and a court can rely on a witness's identification testimony without corroboration if it finds the witness to be particularly credible.
application: The Court found no reason to disbelieve the testimony of PW-17, who had identified an accused in the TIP.

It dismissed the appellants' challenge to the TIP's legality as an "ingenuity in this appeal," emphasizing that no such questions were put to the Magistrate who conducted the parade during his cross-examination at trial.
The Court noted that the argument about a witness seeing the accused beforehand was of "no relevance" as there was no delay in the TIP that would invalidate it.

The Court also highlighted that even in an instance where a TIP was not conducted for an accused, the in-court identification was still deemed reliable, reinforcing that the TIP is a corroborative tool, not an absolute necessity.

The Court found that the identification evidence from the TIP was strongly supported by other corroborating evidence, such as the recovery of the vehicle and money, which solidified the involvement of the accused.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Test Identification Parade (TIP) was correctly relied upon. It found the witness identification to be credible, upheld the lower courts' findings that the parade was without blemish, and dismissed the appellants' challenges to its validity because they were not raised during the trial. The Court further held that the TIP served as valid corroboration for the in-court identification, which was also supported by other significant evidence.

issue.issue_text: Whether an omission to frame, irregularity in the charge, or misjoinder of charges would invalidate a sentence passed by a court of competent jurisdiction.

facts: The appellant (A-8) was convicted under Section 364A/34 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC).
However, the formal charges framed against him were only under Sections 368 and 412 of the IPC.
The appellant's lawyer argued that his conviction under Section 364A/34 was legally untenable because a specific charge for that offense had not been framed against him.
law: The court relied on Section 464 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).
This section states that a sentence passed by a competent court is not invalid due to an omission to frame a charge, or any irregularity or misjoinder in the charge.
The only exception to this rule is if the court concludes that the error has resulted in a "failure of justice."
application: The court applied the principle of Section 464 to the appellant's situation.
It found that no prejudice or failure of justice had been caused to the appellant (A-8) by the irregularity in the charge.
The court reasoned that the appellant knew the essential elements and substance of the charge that was levelled against him, even if the specific section number was not formally framed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that under Section 464 of the Cr.P.C., the irregularity in the charge did not invalidate the sentence because it had not caused a failure of justice or prejudice to the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an omission to frame, irregularity in the charge, or misjoinder of charges would invalidate a sentence passed by a court of competent jurisdiction.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued against the procedural irregularity of re-examining witnesses (PW-1 to PW-6) after the consolidation of the chargesheet.
respondent_arguments: The re-examination of witnesses was a necessary step taken in the interest of the appellant, as he was not named in the first chargesheet and was not present for the initial examination.
The appellant was given a full opportunity to cross-examine these witnesses, and no prejudice was caused, as their depositions remained the same on both occasions.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The inference of common intention should never be reached unless it is a necessary inference deducible from the circumstances of the case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the procedural irregularity of re-examining witnesses did not invalidate the conviction because no prejudice was caused to the appellant. The appellant was afforded a full opportunity to cross-examine these witnesses, and their depositions remained consistent across both examinations, thereby negating any claim of an unfair trial.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied a prejudice test to the alleged procedural irregularity, focusing on whether the appellant's ability to mount a fair defense was compromised, rather than on the mere existence of the irregularity itself.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument regarding the procedural irregularity of re-examining witnesses was rejected because the court found no prejudice was caused to him.
The court determined that the appellant was given a full opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses in question.
The court noted that the depositions of the witnesses remained the same on both occasions, which undermined the appellant's claim of prejudice.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that the re-examination of witnesses caused no prejudice, as the appellant was given a full opportunity for cross-examination.
The court accepted the respondent's position, finding merit in the fact that the witnesses' depositions were consistent in both instances.
The court affirmed the lower court's reliance on the Test Identification Parade, stating it was correctly relied upon, although it did not elaborate on the reasoning for this conclusion.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning prioritizes substantive justice over procedural technicalities, indicating that a conviction will not be overturned for a procedural error unless it can be shown to have caused actual prejudice to the accused.
